'''Joel Rosenbaum''' (born October 4, 1933) is a professor of [[cell biology]] at [[Yale University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.yale.edu/rosenbaum/ |title=The Laboratory of Dr. Joel Rosenbaum |access-date=2009-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090418031122/http://www.yale.edu/rosenbaum/ |archive-date=2009-04-18 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tf09BCmodB0C&q=%22Rosenbaum,+Joel+L*%22|title = American Men & Women of Science: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences|isbn = 9780787673987|last1 = Kalte|first1 = Pamela M.|last2 = Nemeh|first2 = Katherine H.|last3 = Schusterbauer|first3 = Noah|year = 2005}}</ref>

Rosenbaum received his bachelor's degree from [[Syracuse University]] in 1955, and later his M.Sc. Ed. from [[St. Lawrence University]] in 1957. He returned later to Syracuse for his master's degree in 1959 and Ph.D. in 1963.<ref name="Current Biology">{{cite journal |last1=Rosenbaum |first1=Joel |title=Q & A |journal=Current Biology |date=January 2005 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=R39–R40 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2004.12.072}}</ref>

His lab at Yale studies [[cilia]] and [[flagella]], small tail-like [[organelle]]s, using the model species [[Chlamydomonas]], a single-cell alga. The lab is best known for its discovery of [[intraflagellar transport]], a vital molecular process now linked to many human diseases, in 1993. Rosenbaum has continued to pursue intraflagellar transport as his main research interest.

Rosenbaum received the [[E.B. Wilson Medal]] from the [[American Society for Cell Biology|ASCB]] in 2006, the highest award given in the field of cell biology.
